articles.title: AI Isn't Just Extracting More Fossil Fuels—It's Unlocking Renewable Energy Too
articles.content:
Although artificial intelligence is drawing criticism for its energy use, it's also being used by firms such as ExxonMobil and BP to unleash new energy production. The research firm Wood Mackenzie even estimates that AI could unlock 1 trillion extra barrels of oil globally by helping companies "wring substantially more oil out of producing reservoirs."
These developments are good news for consumers, but they could have a significant impact on the environment, according to an August paper published in npj Climate Action. The authors find that AI could prolong oil and gas usage, leading to a 0.47–1.8 gigaton increase in annual global carbon dioxide emissions. The lower end of that estimate is comparable to Mexico's annual carbon dioxide emissions, study co-author Holly Alpine told The Wall Street Journal. The higher end is equivalent to about 5 percent of the world's energy emissions from 2024.
The researchers say net emissions reductions cannot occur unless renewables grow four to five times faster than oil and gas. (They do note there are other ways AI could reduce the greenhouse gas footprint of the fossil fuel industry—namely, "methane leak detection or efficiency gains in power generation.")
This is an ambitious task, considering that fossil fuels account for over 80 percent of the world's energy needs and their peak usage is years away. But there are reasons to be optimistic about AI's role in accelerating the use of clean technologies.
In the same way that oil majors are using AI to find their next well, startups are utilizing the technology to unleash geothermal energy. One such company is Zanskar, which uses a combination of AI, advanced drilling methods, and geoscience to "accurately map the Earth's subsurface and develop geothermal resources that have been overlooked or considered too risky."
At the Lightning Dock project in New Mexico—which Zanskar purchased in 2024—the company's technology has reduced surface infrastructure costs by 75 percent and sped up drilling by 35 percent. Zanskar says Lightning Dock is now "home to the most productive pumped geothermal well in the U.S. and quite possibly the world." Late last year, the company discovered "Big Blind," a naturally occurring geothermal system in Nevada with the potential to power 80,000–100,000 homes with reliable carbon-free energy. In January, it closed a $115 million funding round.
Nuclear power is also benefiting from advances in AI. In August, Atomic Canyon released its Nuclear Industry Virtual Assistant with backing from Nvidia. The tool is designed to help nuclear professionals navigate technical and regulatory landscapes, which could lead to more nuclear power being developed and deployed faster. The industry has also seen a wave of investment from tech companies looking to fuel their power-hungry data centers with clean energy. Big Tech firms such as Google, meanwhile, have poured significant resources into renewable and battery storage projects to support data centers and bring more energy to the grid.
AI is here to stay. We should embrace what it is already starting to give us: a cleaner and more abundant energy future.

articles.title: Brickbats: November 2026
articles.content:
In September 2025, a police officer in Pasadena, California, accidentally shot a fellow officer while engaging in what officials called "horseplay" with loaded firearms. Dashboard camera video showed that while preparing for their shift in the parking garage, one officer drew his gun and pointed it at an officer seated in a patrol car. That officer then drew his own weapon, which discharged, shooting through the windshield and hitting the other officer in the shoulder.
The Denver City Council voted against letting Key Lime Air lease space at the airport because the charter airline transports immigration detainees for the federal government. That decision risked losing $90 million in federal funding, since airlines must be treated equally. City Attorney Miko Brown reportedly told airport officials to investigate the airline's safety record—not for safety reasons but to retroactively create a legal justification for the vote. A memo written at the time quoted Brown saying, "A bad argument is better than no argument."
Hammond, Louisiana, police officer Denver Golmon faces federal charges for allegedly exposing the identity of a confidential informant in a cockfighting investigation. Golmon's uncle was indicted as part of the investigation; according to court records, Golmon shared videos of the informant that were provided to his uncle's attorneys during discovery, telling the recipients not to disclose where the videos came from.
Brenda Brooks, a former school bus driver in Ohio, received 18 months in jail and five years of probation—the maximum sentence—after pleading guilty to child endangerment and driving under the influence. Brooks drove a bus with elementary schoolchildren on board while impaired. She turned the wrong way when leaving the school, then began swerving across the road and missing stops. One child called her parents for help, and her father had to pull in front of the bus to stop it.
Officials in Culver City, California, banned new fast-food restaurants with drive-thru lanes. The proposal grew out of opposition to a planned In-N-Out Burger location. City leaders and some residents said drive-thrus create more traffic, air pollution from idling cars, and safety problems for pedestrians and cyclists. Opponents in the restaurant industry argued the plan would hurt businesses, since most fast-food sales come through drive-thrus, while disadvantaging large families, the elderly, and people with disabilities. In August, the City Council voted to renew the ban for 10 more months.
The Georgia State Patrol fired four troopers after an internal investigation found they profited from police pursuits by filing personal injury claims against the insurance companies of drivers they chased. Investigators said the troopers used crash reports from pursuits they initiated to seek settlements for claims of stress, anxiety, and soreness, even though they had not reported injuries or sought medical treatment at the time. Some troopers collected tens of thousands of dollars and admitted the claims were a way to supplement their income. Prosecutors were later forced to dismiss 27 DUI cases when the troopers in question were excluded from testifying.
Paul Powlesland led volunteers cleaning up a polluted stream in East London, England. They worked for 10 days, removed over 200 bags of trash, and cleared out thick mud and invasive plants, restoring 250 meters (820 feet) of waterway. Fish, dragonflies, and herons have now returned for the first time in decades, but Powlesland faces up to two years in jail for doing the cleanup without official permits.

articles.title: Brickbat: Turkish Banned
articles.content:
Turkish authorities seized control of Halk TV, a popular pro-opposition television station based in Istanbul. Police raided its headquarters, stopped live broadcasts, and prevented staff from entering the building. A court appointed a government administrator to run the station and other companies linked to its owner, Cafer Mahiroğlu, who is being investigated for bribery, money laundering, and rigging public contracts. Mahiroğlu, who lives abroad, denied the accusations. After the takeover, the station stopped airing live news and instead broadcast music and documentaries, while authorities also ordered its social media accounts blocked in Turkey. The seizure came as Halk TV was covering corruption allegations involving figures linked to President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan's ruling party and the trial of imprisoned Istanbul Mayor Ekrem İmamoğlu.

articles.title: Some Reflections On The Lateral Hiring Market
articles.content:
Every year, professors move from lower-ranked institutions to higher-ranked institutions. But for the lateral market to sustain itself, schools have to continue to play the game: recruit laterals, hoping they improve the school's standing before they move onto greener pastures.
One way to measure this market is to analyze the track record of a new school that built its faculty from scratch. Over the past quarter century, the American Bar Association has granted provisional accreditation to about 20 law schools. Only three of those institutions have cracked the top 100 U.S. News rankings. Last year, FIU was at #77 and Drexel was at #82. U.C. Irvine, founded in 2007, is the outlier. The new state school has hovered between #20 and #40 over the past decade. A lot of the credit should go to Founding Dean Erwin Chemerinsky. But even after Chemerinsky departed for Berkeley in 2017, the rankings have stayed fairly consistent.
Starting from a blank slate, Irvine was able to build a faculty from the ground up, using both entry-level hires as well as laterals. I thought it might be worthwhile to analyze lateral hires and departures from Irvine over the past two decades. Here, I owe a debt to Brian Leiter and Dan Filler, who have charted these moves since 2006. Many of the posts on the Faculty Lounge, Concurring Opinions, and Leiter Reports can now be found on the Internet Archive.
I include the raw results below the jump. Here, I will offer some broader observations about the lateral hiring market. I don't think these patterns are limited to Irvine, but that institution is a useful measuring stick because it started so recently. All of my counts here are tentative. Please let me know if there are any errors.
By my count, between 2008 and 2026, at Irvine there were a total of about 40 lateral hires (including two deans).
Between 2008 and 2026, sixteen of these forty lateral hires later departed. Here, I will note the year they were hired and the year they departed.
- Erwin Chemerinsky (Hired in 2008, lateraled to Berkeley in 2017)
- Catherine Fisk (Hired in 2008, lateraled to Berkeley in 2017)
- Jennifer Chacon (Hired in 2009, lateraled to UCLA in 2018)
- Christopher Tomlins (Hired in 2009, lateraled to Berkeley in 2018)
- Olufunmilayo Arewa (Hired in 2009, lateraled to Temple University in 2014)
- Rick Hasen (Hired in 2011, lateraled to UCLA in 2022)
- Douglas NeJaime (Hired in 2013, lateraled to UCLA in 2015)
- Michele B. Goodwin (Hired in 2014, lateraled to Georgetown in 2023)
- Gregory Shaffer (Hired in 2014, lateraled to Georgetown in 2023)
- Sarah Lawsky (Hired in 2010, lateraled to Northwestern in 2016)
- Alexandra Natapoff (Hired in 2017, lateraled to Harvard in 2020)
- David S. Law (Hired in 2019, lateraled to Virginia in 2020)
- Rachel Moran (Hired in 2019, lateraled to Texas A&M in 2023)
- Aziza Ahmed (Hired in 2021, lateraled to Boston University in 2022)
- Jamelia Morgan (Hired in 2021, lateraled to Northwestern in 2022)
- Courtney Cahill (Hired in 2022, lateraled to USC in 2026).
In most of these moves, the professor transferred to a higher-ranked school. The average duration of a lateral hire who departed was about six years.
I exclude in this count two professors (L. Song Richardson and Mario Barnes) who departed for administrative positions, but then returned to Irvine. I also exclude Katie Porter who left teaching to serve in the House, but then returned to the faculty. Those aren't exactly laterals in the traditional sense of the term.
At least four of the lateral hires seem to have taken emeritus status: Bryant Garth, Kaaryn Gustafson, Robert Solomon, and Grace Tonner. As best as I can tell, sixteen recruited laterals are still teaching in a full-time status at Irvine: Christopher Leslie, Tony Reese, Mario Barnes, Katherine Porter, Sameer Ashar, Kenneth W. Simons, Victor Fleischer, Ji Li, Austen Parrish (Dean), Veena Dubal, Kevin Haeberle, Ari Waldman, Robert S. Chang, Andrew Gold, Trevor G. Reed, and Charles Tyler.
If my math is right, out of a total of forty laterals, twenty-four remained and sixteen departed. The departure rate of hired laterals is about 40%. Or, you might say the retention rate is 60%, but that number is harder to rely on because some professors took emeritus status or retired, so were not really on the move.
Moreover, based on my count, there are four professors that Irvine hired on the entry-level market who lateraled out of Irvine: Alejandro Camacho (UCLA), Seth Davis (Berkeley), Jonathan Glater (Berkeley), and Leah Litman (Michigan). If you factor in these departures, the retention rate is even lower.
In an ideal world, the number of lateral hires should far exceed the number of lateral departures. Schools that recruit scholars should be able to retain them. But the world is far from ideal. Professors who lateral to one school will often be recruited elsewhere. Indeed, I think it is a positive that a school recruits and develops scholars who go onto other institutions. More realistically, the number of lateral hires should roughly match the number of lateral departures to keep the faculty at parity: for every lateral that departs another lateral should be hired. At least at Irvine, the number of lateral hires that remained is fairly close to the number of lateral hires that depart. I don't know how Irvine's retention rate compares to other schools. This is something I might compute in the future.
Still, with all of those caveats, to keep a law school's reputation at parity, the rate of lateral departures needs to approximate the rate of lateral hires. If more scholars depart, and cannot be replaced, a school's standing might drop. Indeed, the public might wonder why so many scholars are heading for the door. One might reply that new scholars can be recruited through entry-level hiring. The entry-level market can be unpredictable, and junior scholars can take many years to develop. And again, those entry-level hires who make a name for themselves are likely to be recruited by a higher-ranked institution. It's hard to keep home-grown talent, unless the school either pays up, or the professor has some personal reason to stay.
Another premise is that laterals are expensive. It often takes a lot of money to persuade a professor to move their family from a place they built a strong reputation. Very often professors will sign a retention bonus to promise they will stay at a new law school for a few years. But once those contractual terms lapse, the professor can move up to another school that will pay a greater sum. This happens all the time.
I welcome comments, feedback, and corrections.

In most of these moves, the professor transferred to a higher-ranked school. The average duration of a lateral hire who departed was about six years.

I exclude in this count two professors (L. Song Richardson and Mario Barnes) who departed for administrative positions, but then returned to Irvine. I also exclude Katie Porter who left teaching to serve in the House, but then returned to the faculty. Those aren't exactly laterals in the traditional sense of the term.

At least four of the lateral hires seem to have taken emeritus status: Bryant Garth, Kaaryn Gustafson, Robert Solomon, and Grace Tonner. As best as I can tell, sixteen recruited laterals are still teaching in a full-time status at Irvine: Christopher Leslie, Tony Reese, Mario Barnes, Katherine Porter, Sameer Ashar, Kenneth W. Simons, Victor Fleischer, Ji Li, Austen Parrish (Dean), Veena Dubal, Kevin Haeberle, Ari Waldman, Robert S. Chang, Andrew Gold, Trevor G. Reed, and Charles Tyler.

If my math is right, out of a total of forty laterals, twenty-four remained and sixteen departed. The departure rate of hired laterals is about 40%. Or, you might say the retention rate is 60%, but that number is harder to rely on because some professors took emeritus status or retired, so were not really on the move.

Moreover, based on my count, there are four professors that Irvine hired on the entry-level market who lateraled out of Irvine: Alejandro Camacho (UCLA), Seth Davis (Berkeley), Jonathan Glater (Berkeley), and Leah Litman (Michigan). If you factor in these departures, the retention rate is even lower.

In an ideal world, the number of lateral hires should far exceed the number of lateral departures. Schools that recruit scholars should be able to retain them. But the world is far from ideal. Professors who lateral to one school will often be recruited elsewhere. Indeed, I think it is a positive that a school recruits and develops scholars who go onto other institutions. More realistically, the number of lateral hires should roughly match the number of lateral departures to keep the faculty at parity: for every lateral that departs another lateral should be hired. At least at Irvine, the number of lateral hires that remained is fairly close to the number of lateral hires that depart. I don't know how Irvine's retention rate compares to other schools. This is something I might compute in the future.

Still, with all of those caveats, to keep a law school's reputation at parity, the rate of lateral departures needs to approximate the rate of lateral hires. If more scholars depart, and cannot be replaced, a school's standing might drop. Indeed, the public might wonder why so many scholars are heading for the door. One might reply that new scholars can be recruited through entry-level hiring. The entry-level market can be unpredictable, and junior scholars can take many years to develop. And again, those entry-level hires who make a name for themselves are likely to be recruited by a higher-ranked institution. It's hard to keep home-grown talent, unless the school either pays up, or the professor has some personal reason to stay.

Another premise is that laterals are expensive. It often takes a lot of money to persuade a professor to move their family from a place they built a strong reputation. Very often professors will sign a retention bonus to promise they will stay at a new law school for a few years. But once those contractual terms lapse, the professor can move up to another school that will pay a greater sum. This happens all the time.
